OVERHEARD AT EVERY

WHAT THE TEAM COULDN’T STOP TALKING ABOUT THIS WEEK

Turn your effort dial down. Kate’s reaction to a new paper https://every.?ev_audience=free from Johns Hopkins and Together AI: “Effort level!!” The researchers tested the reasoning-effort setting built into Claude Code, Codex, and ChatGPT. Maximum effort raised accuracy overall, but it often failed tasks that low effort had solved, and on easy tasks it cost up to 42 times as much. Their fix: Start at the lowest setting and raise it only after a checked failure.

The coding interview is dead, at least on one Anthropic team. Felix Rieseberg, an engineering manager at Anthropic, wrote this week https://every.?ev_audience=free that he stopped giving coding interviews because Claude now beats candidates at the small challenges they test. His bigger point is that newer engineers can now build a working prototype over a weekend instead of waiting years for permission. Engineer Lee Knowlton called it “another banger.” For now, Felix looks for small prototypes that show taste.

The Arc breakup continues. Head of social Becky Isjwara, a self-described “arc loyalist,” switched to Dia after it opened the FigJam from her call and grouped it with the Google Meet tab. Lee isn’t there yet: Dia is “like arc but uglier.” Customer support specialist Waqqas Mir moved to Brave instead: “cant go through another breakup with a browser.”—Grant Harvey https://every.?ev_audience=free

PROTOCOLS

From this week’s stories, 13 skills to try.

GET AGENTS TO CITE YOUR WORK

From Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free’s “How to Get AI Agents to Recommend Your Articles” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Write the subtitle as the answer. Rewriting both the title and subtitle of Mike’s prompt engineering guide took it from two agent citations in 240 sessions to 240 of 240. The rules https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Bet on one post per topic. Agents tend to cite a single post from a site on each topic, so pick the one you want to win and make its subtitle the clearest answer. The rule https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Test your titles with agent-pass. Mike’s Claude Code skill reviews a post’s title and subtitle, suggests truthful rewrites, and tests them against real agents. The skill https://every.?ev_audience=free

GET MORE OUT OF NEW MODELS

From Grant Harvey’s “Every Model Has a Six-month Shelf Life Now” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Brief AI on your taste before it vets your idea. Emmy-winning TV writer Fred Graver writes one doc about his inspirations, tastes, and ambitions and another about the project, then asks AI whether the idea really fits his voice. The method https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Give each model its own job. His “very unpleasant” Claude agent holds him to existing commitments, ChatGPT plays an eager film student who checks the basics, and NotebookLM’s podcast hosts supply encouragement. The cast https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Test each new model on one hard task. When a model ships, read the Vibe Check https://every.?ev_audience=free, then try it on your personal benchmark: one hard task you know well. The habit https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Ask AI which of your skills to sell first. Mike’s shoggoth strategy is to market yourself on one clear specialty and keep your generalist skills behind it. His prompt asks your agent to list your 10 strongest skills and pick the one you should lead with when people ask what you do. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free

WORK ALONGSIDE AN AI COWORKER

From Grant Harvey’s “My First Week With an AI Coworker” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Check your blind spots. Ask your team’s agent, “What can you do for me that I haven’t tried yet?” Grant’s agent found his biggest gap in seconds: He had no scheduled tasks. The prompts https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Check the agent’s sources. Before you act on an agent’s answer, ask, “What’s your source, and when was it last updated?” The prompts https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Keep a running tally of what you owe people. Staff writer Laura Entis https://every.?ev_audience=free’s Dot collects the requests she agrees to in passing and messages her about deadlines, promised feedback, and decisions waiting on her. The prompt https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Pick the format before you write the doc. Head of platform Willie Williams https://every.?ev_audience=free gives AI an existing proposal or spreadsheet, says who it’s for, and asks for it as a video, webpage, or interactive plan modeled on a reference he likes. The steps https://every.?ev_audience=free

DECIDE WHAT TO HAND YOUR CODING AGENTS

From Loren Stewart https://every.?ev_audience=free’s “What Karl Marx Would Say About My Coding Agents” https://every.?ev_audience=free

 * Give each task a mode. Engineer Loren Stewart lets agents run on their own for routine work like his morning briefing, adds checkpoints before key decisions on systems he wants to understand, and codes by hand when he wants to learn something new. The modes https://every.?ev_audience=free
 * Make the agent’s code teach you. For code he didn’t write, he asks an agent to write checks for the parts he wants to understand, then works through them in a debugger to see how the code works and what the checks missed. The method https://every.?ev_audience=free

ALIGNMENT

Professor Oak, unmasked. After six years of anonymous X biotech commentary, “Professor Oak” revealed himself this week https://every.?ev_audience=free to be Cody Tranbarger, founder of Mithril Medicine. He did so by announcing that Anthropic had acquired his company, which is a beautifully spectacular way to introduce yourself to the world.

As Mithril’s sole founder and employee, Cody used Claude to help coordinate work across 11 outside laboratories. According to Anthropic https://every.?ev_audience=free, a potential treatment for a rare muscular dystrophy went from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. He now plans to start several more programs inside Anthropic to see how far Claude can extend his own expertise.

Anthropic is most likely going to turn that experience into better tools to sell through its relationships with pharmaceutical companies while applying the same improvements to its own drug programs.

For other founders reading the news, the question becomes how much company they need to build around their expertise. If Claude can reliably coordinate outside laboratories and take on more of the scientific work itself, a small team might be able to pursue several programs without the need to scale hiring.

Clinical trials will still take years, but expert drug hunters may be able to reach the point where a treatment attracts a buyer or further investment with far less time and money. Whether Claude can make that happen often enough and on compressed timelines will determine if these lean biotechs become a solid venture bet.—Ashwin Sharma https://every.?ev_audience=free
